summary.text: The proof reduces both factors to explicit \(p\)-adic valuation sums: the gcd product contributes \(\sum_{i\ge1}\lfloor m/p^i\rfloor^2\), while the factorial product contributes \(\sum_{i\ge1}\sum_{r\ge1}r\lfloor \lfloor m/p^i\rfloor/r\rfloor\); the termwise bound \(\sum_{r\le N}r\lfloor N/r\rfloor\le N^2\) also proves the latter product divides the former. Since \(\lfloor(np+k)/p^i\rfloor=\lfloor np/p^i\rfloor\) for every \(i\ge1\) when \(k<p\), both valuation sums—and hence their difference—are unchanged.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 A(m)=\prod_{1\le j\le m}\prod_{1\le k\le m}\gcd(j,k),
 \qquad
 B(m)=\prod_{1\le k\le m}\left(\left\lfloor\frac m k\right\rfloor !\right)^k.
\]
Thus the sequence in the question is
\[
 a(m)=\frac{A(m)}{B(m)}.
\]
We will first show that this quotient is an integer and obtain formulas for its prime valuations. For a prime \(q\), write \(\nu_q(r)\) for the exponent of \(q\) in a positive integer \(r\).

We repeatedly use the elementary floor-division identity
\[
 \left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor u/v\rfloor}{w}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac{u}{vw}\right\rfloor
 \tag{1}
\]
for positive integers \(v,w\). In particular, the two divisors can be interchanged:
\[
 \left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor u/v\rfloor}{w}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor u/w\rfloor}{v}\right\rfloor.
 \tag{2}
\]

First consider the numerator. Since
\[
 \nu_q(\gcd(j,k))=\min(\nu_q(j),\nu_q(k)),
\]
and since for nonnegative integers \(r,s\)
\[
 \min(r,s)=\sum_{i\ge1}{\bf 1}_{i\le r}{\bf 1}_{i\le s},
\]
we have
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \nu_q(A(m))
 &=\sum_{j=1}^m\sum_{k=1}^m\min(\nu_q(j),\nu_q(k))\\
 &=\sum_{i\ge1}
   \left(\sum_{j=1}^m {\bf 1}_{q^i\mid j}\right)
   \left(\sum_{k=1}^m {\bf 1}_{q^i\mid k}\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
The number of multiples of \(q^i\) among \(1,\ldots,m\) is \(\lfloor m/q^i\rfloor\). Consequently
\[
 \boxed{\displaystyle
 \nu_q(A(m))=\sum_{i\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac{m}{q^i}\right\rfloor^2.}
 \tag{3}
\]
All sums written with \(i\ge1\) are in fact finite, because their terms vanish once \(q^i>m\).

For the denominator, additivity of valuations on products and the formula
\[
 \nu_q(t!)=\sum_{i\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac{t}{q^i}\right\rfloor
\]
give
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \nu_q(B(m))
 &=\sum_{k=1}^m k\,\nu_q\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac m k\right\rfloor!\right)\\
 &=\sum_{k=1}^m k\sum_{i\ge1}
   \left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor m/k\rfloor}{q^i}\right\rfloor\\
 &=\sum_{i\ge1}\sum_{k=1}^m k
   \left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor m/k\rfloor}{q^i}\right\rfloor.
\end{aligned}
\]
Using (2), and putting
\[
 N_i(m)=\left\lfloor\frac{m}{q^i}\right\rfloor,
\]
this becomes
\[
 \boxed{\displaystyle
 \nu_q(B(m))=\sum_{i\ge1}\sum_{k=1}^m
 k\left\lfloor\frac{N_i(m)}{k}\right\rfloor.}
 \tag{4}
\]

We next prove that \(B(m)\mid A(m)\). Fix a prime \(q\) and a level \(i\ge1\), and abbreviate \(N=N_i(m)\). If \(k>N\), then \(\lfloor N/k\rfloor=0\), so
\[
 \sum_{k=1}^m k\left\lfloor\frac Nk\right\rfloor
 =\sum_{k=1}^N k\left\lfloor\frac Nk\right\rfloor.
\]
For each \(1\le k\le N\),
\[
 k\left\lfloor\frac Nk\right\rfloor\le N.
\]
There are \(N\) such terms, and hence
\[
 \sum_{k=1}^m k\left\lfloor\frac Nk\right\rfloor\le N^2.
 \tag{5}
\]
Summing (5) over \(i\), and comparing (3) with (4), yields
\[
 \nu_q(B(m))\le \nu_q(A(m))
\]
for every prime \(q\). Both \(A(m)\) and \(B(m)\) are positive: every gcd occurring in \(A(m)\) is positive, and every factorial occurring in \(B(m)\) is positive. The prime-exponent criterion for divisibility therefore gives
\[
 B(m)\mid A(m).
 \tag{6}
\]
Thus \(a(m)=A(m)/B(m)\) is indeed an integer, and for every prime \(q\),
\[
 \boxed{\displaystyle
 \nu_q(a(m))=\nu_q(A(m))-\nu_q(B(m)).}
 \tag{7}
\]

We now prove the asserted constancy. Fix a positive integer \(n\), a prime \(p\), and an integer \(x\) with \(0\le x<p\). Set
\[
 m_0=np,\qquad m_x=np+x.
\]
The key observation is that for every \(i\ge1\),
\[
 \left\lfloor\frac{np+x}{p^i}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac{np}{p^i}\right\rfloor.
 \tag{8}
\]
Indeed, division by \(p\) first gives
\[
 \left\lfloor\frac{np+x}{p}\right\rfloor=n
 =\left\lfloor\frac{np}{p}\right\rfloor,
\]
because \(0\le x<p\). Dividing these equal quotients a further \(i-1\) times by \(p\), using (1), proves (8).

Applying the numerator formula (3) with \(q=p\), every summand for \(m_x\) agrees with the corresponding summand for \(m_0\) by (8). Therefore
\[
 \nu_p(A(np+x))=\nu_p(A(np)).
 \tag{9}
\]

We similarly compare the denominator valuations. Formula (4), now with \(q=p\), says
\[
 \nu_p(B(m))=
 \sum_{i\ge1}\sum_{k=1}^m
 k\left\lfloor\frac{N_i(m)}{k}\right\rfloor,
 \qquad
 N_i(m)=\left\lfloor\frac m{p^i}\right\rfloor.
 \tag{10}
\]
By (8),
\[
 N_i(np+x)=N_i(np)
 \tag{11}
\]
for every \(i\ge1\). Thus the terms in (10) with \(1\le k\le np\) are identical for \(m=np+x\) and \(m=np\). The only apparently new terms are those with
\[
 np<k\le np+x.
\]
But for every \(i\ge1\),
\[
 N_i(np)=\left\lfloor\frac{np}{p^i}\right\rfloor\le np<k,
\]
so
\[
 \left\lfloor\frac{N_i(np)}k\right\rfloor=0.
\]
By (11), the corresponding quotient for \(np+x\) is also zero. Hence all the added terms vanish, and we conclude that
\[
 \nu_p(B(np+x))=\nu_p(B(np)).
 \tag{12}
\]

Finally, use (7) first at \(m=np+x\) and then at \(m=np\). Equations (9) and (12) give
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \nu_p(a(np+x))
 &=\nu_p(A(np+x))-\nu_p(B(np+x))\\
 &=\nu_p(A(np))-\nu_p(B(np))\\
 &=\nu_p(a(np)).
\end{aligned}
\]
This holds for every \(x\) with \(0\le x<p\). Taking \(x=0,1,\ldots,p-1\) proves
\[
 \operatorname{ord}_p(a(np))=
 \operatorname{ord}_p(a(np+1))=\cdots=
 \operatorname{ord}_p(a(np+p-1)),
\]
as required.
